flashcards.q: What are the three distinct things transpile() does?
flashcards.a: Basis translation (rewrite gates into the target's native gate set), routing (insert SWAP gates for limited qubit connectivity), and optimization (optimization_level=0-3, reducing gate count/depth).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between Statevector simulation and shot-based (Sampler) simulation?
flashcards.a: Statevector gives the exact amplitude vector with no sampling noise, simulation-only. Sampler returns a counts dictionary from repeated executions with statistical noise shrinking as 1/√shots — this is what real hardware actually returns.

flashcards.q: Why can real quantum hardware never return a Statevector object?
flashcards.a: Measurement is destructive and collapses the state (Born rule) — real devices only ever produce classical bitstrings from repeated executions, never the underlying amplitude vector directly.

flashcards.q: How does statistical shot noise scale with the number of shots?
flashcards.a: Standard error ~ √(p(1-p)/shots), i.e. 1/√shots. 10x more shots buys ~√10≈3.16x tighter precision, not 10x. Verified: deviation from p=0.5 fell from 0.10 at 10 shots to 0.0009 at 100,000 shots.

flashcards.q: How do you distinguish statistical shot noise from systematic hardware noise in a histogram?
flashcards.a: Statistical noise shrinks predictably as 1/√shots with more shots. Systematic noise (decoherence, gate error, readout error) persists regardless of shot count — a deviation that doesn't shrink with more shots points to real hardware noise, not sampling.

flashcards.q: What replaced Qiskit's execute() function, and when?
flashcards.a: The primitives model — Sampler (measurement-outcome distributions) and Estimator (expectation values) — replaced execute() starting with Qiskit 1.0 (February 2024). They work identically on local simulators and real IBM hardware.

flashcards.q: What is a 'fake backend' noise model in AerSimulator and why use it?
flashcards.a: It loads real calibration data (gate error rates, T1/T2, readout error) from an actual IBM device snapshot, letting you estimate realistic circuit performance locally with no queue wait or cost before submitting to real hardware.

flashcards.q: Why should a Clifford-only circuit (H, S, CNOT) use a stabilizer simulator instead of a general statevector simulator?
flashcards.a: Gottesman-Knill (module 2) means Clifford-only circuits are classically efficiently simulable; a dedicated stabilizer simulator handles thousands of qubits in polynomial time by tracking stabilizer generators, whereas a general simulator still does full O(2^n) linear algebra.

flashcards.q: What breaks a stabilizer simulator's polynomial-time advantage?
flashcards.a: Introducing even one non-Clifford gate (e.g. T) — stabilizer simulators are built specifically for Clifford operations and fail or require a fundamentally more expensive technique the moment T gates appear.

flashcards.q: What does a mismatch between a counts dictionary's total and the requested shot count usually indicate?
flashcards.a: Missing measure() calls on some qubits, or measuring into fewer classical bits than qubits, silently dropping outcomes.

flashcards.q: What is the recommended debugging order when a circuit's real-hardware results don't match expectations?
flashcards.a: Verify circuit logic against noiseless Statevector simulation first (zero noise, exact amplitudes visible). Only after confirming logical correctness there, move to shot-based simulation, then real hardware, to isolate whether a discrepancy is a logic bug versus a hardware/transpilation issue.

flashcards.q: What is the maintenance status of qiskit-aer as of 2026?
flashcards.a: Under reduced maintenance — critical bug fixes only, feature requests backlogged — reflecting IBM's shifted investment toward cloud Runtime primitives and hardware-facing tooling, though it remains fully usable for local simulation.
